title: Was a USB drive connected to this Windows computer?
lead: Windows keeps a record each time a USB storage device is plugged in. This workflow shows how to find which device it was, when it was connected, which drive letter it got, which user account used it, and what was opened from it.
time: 1 to 2 hours on the practice image
evidence: A disk image of a Windows computer
answers: Which USB storage devices were connected (make, model, serial number)
When each one was first and last connected
Which drive letter and volume name it had
Which user account had it mounted
Which files or folders were opened from it
need: A forensic image of the Windows computer, or a practice image (see the practice section on this page)
A Windows workstation for the analysis tools
Free disk space of about three times the image size

steps.title: Work on an image, never the original
steps.text: If you are starting from a real disk, make a forensic image through a write blocker and note its hash value. Every later step uses the image. For practice, download a public test image instead.

steps.title: Get a first answer with Autopsy
steps.text: Create a case, add the image as a data source and run the Recent Activity module. When it finishes, open the result list named USB Device Attached (older versions call it Devices Attached). You get the make, model and device ID of each device and a date and time. Treat this as a lead to confirm in the next steps.

steps.title: Export the files that hold the evidence
steps.text: From the image, export the registry hives and logs listed below. In Autopsy, right-click a file and choose Extract File(s). Export one NTUSER.DAT for each user profile.

steps.title: Identify the device
steps.text: Open the SYSTEM hive in Registry Explorer and go to the USBSTOR key. Each sub-key is one device model, named with the vendor, product and revision. The key under it is the serial number. If the second character of the serial number is &, Windows made that value up because the device did not report a serial number of its own, so it cannot identify one physical device.

steps.title: Find the drive letter and volume name
steps.text: MountedDevices in the SYSTEM hive maps drive letters and volume GUIDs to devices. It keeps only the last device that used each letter. The Windows Portable Devices key in the SOFTWARE hive stores a friendly name, which is often the volume label.

steps.title: Work out when it was connected
steps.text: Search setupapi.dev.log for the serial number. The first entry is the time Windows first installed the device, written in the computer's local time. On Windows 8 and later, the device's Properties key in USBSTOR also stores first install, last connected and last removed times. On Windows 10 and later, the Partition/Diagnostic event log records event 1006 for each connect and disconnect.
steps.note: Registry times are in UTC. setupapi.dev.log uses local time. Write down the time zone of the computer before you compare them.

steps.title: Link the device to a user account
steps.text: Open each user's NTUSER.DAT and look at MountPoints2. If the volume GUID you found in MountedDevices appears there, that account was logged in while the volume was mounted.

steps.title: Find what was opened from the drive
steps.text: Shortcut (LNK) files, jump lists and shellbags record files and folders the user opened, together with the drive letter and volume serial number. Matching the volume serial number ties those files to the USB drive. Autopsy lists shortcut files under Recent Documents. The LNK, jump list and shellbag parsers in Eric Zimmerman's Tools give more detail.

steps.title: Cross-check and write it down
steps.text: Confirm each fact from two places, for example Autopsy and Registry Explorer, or the registry and the event log. In your notes, record the tool name and version, the file each value came from, and the time zone.

artifacts.name: USBSTOR
artifacts.tells: Vendor, product and serial number of each USB storage device

artifacts.name: MountedDevices
artifacts.tells: The last device that used each drive letter, and volume GUIDs

artifacts.name: Windows Portable Devices
artifacts.tells: Friendly name, often the volume label

artifacts.name: MountPoints2
artifacts.tells: Which user account had the volume mounted

artifacts.name: setupapi.dev.log
artifacts.tells: First time the device was installed (local time)

artifacts.name: Partition/Diagnostic log, event 1006
artifacts.tells: Each connect and disconnect, sometimes with the volume serial number

artifacts.name: LNK files, jump lists, shellbags
artifacts.where: User profile and user registry hives
artifacts.tells: Files and folders opened, with drive letter and volume serial number

limits: A device record shows that a device was connected. It does not show who physically plugged it in.
It does not show that files were copied. Copying needs its own evidence, such as opened-file records or an examination of the USB drive itself.
Records can be missing. Cleaning tools remove them, and the Partition/Diagnostic log can be cleared by major Windows updates.
Some sources keep only the first and the last time, not every connection.
Phones and cameras that connect as media devices leave different traces from USB storage drives.
Key names and available timestamps change between Windows versions. Check what applies to the version you are examining.

practice.name: NIST CFReDS: Data Leakage Case
practice.text: A simulated intellectual property theft on a Windows 7 computer, with images of the PC and of the removable media. The PC image is about 5 GB to download as a compressed DD image, or about 7.3 GB in E01 format. NIST publishes an answer document, so you can check your result.
practice.task: Try question 22 of the case: "List external storage devices attached to PC." Then compare your list with the published answers.
practice.note: The practice computer runs Windows 7, so the Partition/Diagnostic event log in step 6 will not be there. Everything else in this workflow applies.
